item.content:encoded:
Bobby Witt Jr. is having a down year. He’s running his worst batting line in three seasons. He’s in danger of missing the 20-homer threshold for the first time in his career. A lower back injury in July will also limit him to a career low in games played. Put it together, and Witt is on pace to put up his the lowest WAR total since his 5.9-win 2023 campaign. Oh, and he also grabbed hold of the American League lead in WAR back in July and still hasn’t relinquished it. A down year by Bobby Witt Jr.’s standards is still good enough to make him a deserving MVP.
I don’t know if Witt is going to win his first MVP this year. Ours is the only flavor of WAR in which he leads the AL, and he leads by just a quarter of a win. He ranks third by Baseball Reference’s rWAR and is eighth by Baseball Prospectus’ WARP. Yordan Alvarez leads all of baseball in WARP because he’s hitting like, well, Yordan Alvarez and staying healthy like, well, someone other than Yordan Alvarez. Cam Schlittler leads the AL in Baseball Reference WAR, and he’s been so dominant that he deserves consideration for the Cy Young-MVP combo — if only he’d pitched just 23 fewer innings last year, he could’ve gone for the trifecta with Rookie of the Year. Kevin McGonigle has played like an MVP from the moment he arrived in Detroit, and Junior Caminero has surpassed 40 home runs for the second season in a row as a 23-year-old. All of these guys have a case, and they aren’t the only ones who merit inclusion in the discussion:
| Name | fWAR Rk | fWAR | rWAR Rk | rWAR | WARP Rk | WARP | Avg Rk | Avg WAR |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bobby Witt Jr. | 1 | 6.6 | 3 | 6.5 | 8 | 5 | 4 | 6.0 |
| Yordan Alvarez | 2 | 6.4 | 4 | 6.4 | 1 | 7.3 | 2 | 6.7 |
| Cam Schlittler | 3 | 6.1 | 1 | 7 | 3 | 5.8 | 2 | 6.3 |
| Dylan Cease | 4 | 5.5 | 8 | 5.7 | 12 | 4.6 | 8 | 5.3 |
| Miguel Vargas | 5 | 5.2 | 10 | 5.3 | 2 | 5.9 | 6 | 5.5 |
| Junior Caminero | 6 | 5.2 | 7 | 5.7 | 5 | 5.3 | 6 | 5.4 |
| Kevin McGonigle | 7 | 5.1 | 2 | 6.7 | 4 | 5.3 | 4 | 5.7 |
| Randy Arozarena | 8 | 5.1 | 11 | 5.3 | 16 | 4 | 12 | 4.8 |
| Dillon Dingler | 9 | 4.6 | 25 | 4 | 23 | 3.3 | 19 | 4.0 |
| Drew Rasmussen | 10 | 4.6 | 21 | 4.2 | 13 | 4.4 | 15 | 4.4 |
| Reid Detmers | 11 | 4.6 | 35 | 3.7 | 11 | 4.7 | 19 | 4.3 |
| Parker Messick | 13 | 4.6 | 6 | 5.8 | 9 | 4.8 | 9 | 5.1 |
| Pete Alonso | 14 | 4.2 | 18 | 4.3 | 6 | 5.3 | 13 | 4.6 |
| Ceddanne Rafaela | 21 | 3.9 | 9 | 5.4 | 94 | 1.7 | 41 | 3.7 |
| Gavin Williams | 27 | 3.7 | 46 | 3.1 | 7 | 5.2 | 27 | 4.0 |
| Wilyer Abreu | 32 | 3.4 | 5 | 5.8 | 20 | 3.6 | 19 | 4.3 |
| Mike Trout | 40 | 3.2 | 28 | 3.9 | 10 | 4.8 | 26 | 4.0 |
Pete Crow-Armstrong, Jacob Misiorowski, Schlittler, McGonigle and JJ Wetherholt have made the AL MVP the only major award that’s really in question). If you want to read a particularly good example, you should check out the one Mario Delgado Genzor wrote for Baseball Prospectus on Friday. I want to focus on something slightly different — namely, how good Witt has already been in years when he missed out on an MVP and how unusual it would be for him to win it this year.
(A quick note before we get into it: We’re about to spend a lot of time talking about WAR. I know I mentioned rWAR and WARP earlier. They’re an important piece of the puzzle, especially due to the outsized effect rWAR in particular has on the MVP conversation, but from here on out, we’re sticking with good old FanGraphs WAR.)
This is Witt’s fifth major league season, and you could argue that it’s his fourth consecutive MVP-caliber campaign. Mind you, that argument would focus only on 2022, in which he put up 5.9 WAR, good for 10th in the majors. There’s no argument to be had about the 2024 and 2025 seasons. That said, along with Shohei Ohtani’s combined 9.2-WAR 2022 sesaon, they are the two most valuable seasons this decade for which a position player did not win an MVP. In 2024, Witt ran a 169 wRC+, stole 31 bases, and put up a Fielding Run Value of 11, fourth among all shortstops. That was good for 10.5 WAR, and it took the best season of Aaron Judge’s career – 58 home runs, a 19% walk rate, and a .322 batting average – to beat him. In 2025, Witt put up 8.0 WAR with a 130 wRC+, 38 steals, and 20 FRV, the best mark among all shortstops. Again, he was bested by a 10-win season from Judge and Cal Raleigh’s 60-homer campaign. Witt has never received a first place MVP vote.
Crow-Armstrong, who has the National League MVP all but locked down, gives us a great example of what it normally takes to win an MVP award. He may even finish with 10.5 WAR through his excellence in all three phases of the game, just like Witt did in 2024. Players like Judge, Ohtani, and Mike Trout, whose base level of talent is so high that a healthy campaign is almost sure to keep them a step above the rest of the league, don’t come around all that often. Even when they do come around, they still need to be playing at something close to their peak, and peaks don’t last that long. Until Ohtani, the only player to win more than three MVPs was Barry Bonds, whose regimen for raising and widening his peak has been well documented. Sometimes that’s because of voter fatigue, but often it’s because somebody else popped up with an amazing, undeniable season like PCA’s. Most of the time, the MVP is an already great player for whom everything goes perfectly. They stay healthy and they play not just their best, but over their heads. Think of Ronald Acuña Jr. winning the NL MVP in 2023 with 9.1 WAR, 4.1 more than his next-best total, or Mookie Betts winning the AL MVP in 2018 with 10.2 WAR, 2.8 more than his next-best total.
Generally speaking, since the voting started getting more rigorous in the last couple decades, those are the two categories of players who win MVPs. We see all-time greats who perform like only they are capable of performing, and we see excellent players who put it all together in a blaze of glory. Witt’s 2024 season probably falls into that second category. He wasn’t quite at his defensive or baserunning peak, but he put up his best season at the plate by nearly 40 points of wRC+ and DRC+, and he ended up with an all-timer of a season. His 10.5 WAR tied for the 36th-best position player campaign of all time. His company? Willie Mays and Babe Ruth twice apiece, Barry Bonds, and Rogers Hornsby. Unfortunately, he ran into one of those special players from the first category, in the form of Judge. If Witt had put up those 2024 numbers this year, he’d be en route to a unanimous MVP just like PCA.
But I said “in theory” earlier, and I said it because Witt isn’t done yet. He’s still just 26, and if not for those weeks he missed with back tightness, or a wOBA that’s more than 30 points below his xwOBA, he’d now be wrapping up his third straight seven-plus-win season. He’s elite in every facet of the game and he doesn’t look like he’s in danger of slowing down any time soon. It wouldn’t be much of a shock to see him rediscover his nine- or 10-win form. In other words, there’s at least a chance Witt belongs to that first category of player and not the second.
Earlier I mentioned Acuña and Betts claiming MVPs by putting up the best years of their careers by a long shot. That’s pretty standard. Especially in recent years, it’s awfully rare for a player to take home an MVP award in something other than the best season of their career, unless they also won the MVP in the best year of their career. Leaving those multi-time MVPs out (and excluding 2020 for obvious reasons), here’s the whole list of players who won an MVP in a year that wasn’t their best by fWAR since 2011: Giancarlo Stanton and Paul Goldschmidt.
Goldschmidt put up 6.8 WAR in his 2022 NL MVP season and 7.2 in 2015. In that sense, Goldschmidt fit a third archetype: the established star who doesn’t put up their biggest WAR total, and instead wins MVP as something of a career achievement award. Stanton put up 6.5 WAR in 2017, not quite the 6.8-win campaign he put up in 2014, but he was facing a weaker field, he was more established as a star, and he had the cachet of a 59-homer season. We’re talking about gaps of less than half a win. We had some multi-time winners, but Acuña, Betts, Cody Bellinger, Christian Yelich, Jose Altuve, Kris Bryant, Josh Donaldson, Andrew McCutchen, and Buster Posey all won MVP in the best seasons of their career by fWAR.
Let’s say that Witt does win the MVP this year. For the sake of round numbers, let’s say he closes strong and finishes with 7.0 WAR. That would be just the third-best season of his career, and a full 3.5 WAR below his career-high. Baseball Reference lists MVP winners going back to 1911, and in that time, Witt would become just the ninth position player to win MVP in a season that trailed their best year by such a wide margin. The list of players to do it before him is full of three-time MVPs like Joe DiMaggio, Mickey Mantle, and Mike Schmidt. Not only that, but you’ll note that if Witt does make this list, the only higher number in either column will belong to Mantle:
| Player | MVP Year | MVP WAR | Best Year | Best WAR | Difference |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Frankie Frisch | 1931 | 4.1 | 1927 | 9.7 | 5.6 |
| Mickey Mantle | 1962 | 6.0 | 1956 | 11.5 | 5.5 |
| Willie Stargell | 1979 | 2.7 | 1971 | 8.2 | 5.4 |
| Joe DiMaggio | 1947 | 4.8 | 1941 | 9.7 | 4.9 |
| Freddie Freeman | 2020* | 3.0 | 2023 | 7.7 | 4.7 |
| Robin Yount | 1989 | 5.3 | 1982 | 9.8 | 4.5 |
| Andre Dawson | 1987 | 3.5 | 1982 | 7.3 | 3.8 |
| Mike Schmidt | 1986 | 5.8 | 1974 | 9.4 | 3.6 |
| Roger Peckinpaugh | 1925 | 2.4 | 1919 | 5.9 | 3.5 |
The last person to do so was Robin Yount, who won the AL MVP with 9.8 WAR in 1982, and then again with 5.3 WAR in 1989, long before anybody knew that Total Zone considered him the 11th-worst defender in the majors. This hasn’t happened in nearly 30 years, and Witt is in a very different boat here. He’s not one of the two MVP favorites because his season looks great to the eye but doesn’t fool the advanced metrics. He’s not an aging star who can count on some lifetime-achievement votes. He’s a young gun who’s leading his league in WAR because he excels in every facet of the game.
I realize that this is far from the most meticulous analysis I’ve ever conducted, and that MVP voting is and should be about more than WAR. Still, I hope I’ve put this season in the context it deserves. By our measuring stick, Witt has been the best player in the American League this season. He’s done so despite missing time due to injury. He’s done so despite some bad batted ball luck. And he’s done so despite not even coming close to the highest gear we know he’s got available to him, because that gear is so high that it’s normally reserved for inner-circle Hall of Famers. However the voting goes, Witt’s been in MVP form for three or four years now.
Davy Andrews is a Brooklyn-based musician and a writer at FanGraphs. He can be found on Bluesky @davyandrewsdavy.bsky.social.

item.content:encoded:
The final week of the 2026 regular season has arrived and there is still much to be determined.
While six teams have clinched playoff spots and a few others are close, multiple playoff positions are still up for grabs. And from an individual perspective, there are awards that could be determined in the coming days.
Here’s what is at stake in the final week of the season.
Who will win the AL West and Central?
There’s no telling who will win these two divisions in the American League. The Rays have just about wrapped up the AL East, but the White Sox and Guardians are still battling for the AL Central, while the Rangers and Astros are battling for the West.
This is where things stand. The Rangers lead the Astros by one game in the AL West but Houston won the pivotal tiebreaker against Texas. That means if the two clubs end the season with the same record, the division would go to the Astros.
In the AL Central, the Guardians hold a one-game lead over the White Sox, but Chicago holds the tiebreaker advantage. Any tie between the two clubs means the White Sox would win the division.
Who gets the last AL Wild Card spot?
The AL West and Central battles are directly linked to what’s happening for the final Wild Card spot. It’s very likely that one of those four aforementioned teams will grab the last AL Wild Card spot, unless the Blue Jays have something to say about it. Right now, the White Sox have a fairly comfortable three-game lead over the Blue Jays and Astros.
Could Yordan still win the Triple Crown?
For a while, Yordan Alvarez looked like he might win the MLB Triple Crown, leading the Majors in average, home runs and RBIs. Now, the lefty slugger and presumptive AL MVP winner might merely finish first or second in average, home runs and RBIs. Heading into the final week, Alvarez has a slight edge in average (.313) over Chandler Simpson (.309) and is second in home runs (40) behind Junior Caminero (41) and second in RBIs (99) behind Pete Alonso (105). Alvarez could still snag the AL Triple Crown, but it’ll take a monstrous final week.
Simpson’s unique season and quest for an unusual batting title
Back to Simpson for a second, though. The Rays outfielder is having an excellent season, hitting for average, swiping bases and playing solid outfield defense. What he hasn’t done, though, is hit a single home run. The last hitter to win a batting title without hitting a home run was Rod Carew in 1972. Even if he doesn’t win, he could be the first qualified hitter to bat .300 without a home run since Luis Castillo in 1999.
Will Misiorowski win the ERA title?
It's been a remarkable season for Jacob Misiorowski, who has a 1.86 ERA and 247 strikeouts after Sunday's outing against the Orioles. Assuming he's in line for one more start next weekend -- even if it's abbreviated like his three-inning outing on Sunday -- Misiorowski is in line to join some impressive company. If he can hold his ERA edge over Cam Schlittler's 1.94 mark, he'd join 2021 Corbin Burnes (2.43 ERA in 2021) as the only Brewers to win an ERA title.
If Misiorowski keeps his ERA under two and gets to 250 strikeouts, there's some other fun company he'll join. He'd be just the 13th pitcher (15th instance) since earned runs became official in 1913 to finish a season with a sub-2 ERA and 250-plus strikeouts. The last to do so was Jacob deGrom in 2018.
Will Schwarber or PCA lead the Majors in home runs?
Kyle Schwarber led the National League with 56 home runs last year. As hard as it is to believe, though, Schwarber has never led the Majors in home runs. That could change this year, as the Phillies’ slugger is tied for the MLB lead with 45 homers. The last Phillie to pull that off was Ryan Howard in 2008, when he hit 48 homers and helped lead Philly to a World Series title.
Schwarber, though, has Pete Crow-Armstrong tied with him at the top. The surefire NL MVP has completely taken off this season with 45 homers, 38 stolen bases (more on this shortly), a .949 OPS and his usual excellent center field defense, which has led to an MLB-best 10.5 WAR, per FanGraphs. If PCA surpasses Schwarber, he’d be the first Cub to lead the NL in homers since Sammy Sosa’s 49 homers in 2002 and the first to lead the Majors in long balls since Sosa hit 50 in 2000.
Does PCA get to 40-40?
Crow-Armstrong is making all sorts of history this season. Reaching 10 WAR puts PCA in rarified territory and it seems very likely that the Cubs’ superstar center fielder will be a unanimous MVP winner, something no Cub has ever achieved. Crow-Armstrong is also a mere two stolen bases away from a 40-40 season, something no Cub has done and only six other MLB players have achieved.
Burleson vying to join impressive Cardinals history
Alec Burleson leads the Majors with 111 RBIs, putting him in line for some impressive Cardinals history. He’s looking to become the first Cardinal to lead the National League since Albert Pujols in 2010 and the first to lead the Majors in the category since Joe Torre drove in 137 runs in 1971. His stiffest competition is Cincinnati’s Sal Stewart, who sits at 110 RBIs entering the final week.
How does Verlander's final start go?
Justin Verlander returned to the Tigers for the 2026 season, which will be his final before retiring. Unfortunately, he only made one start in April and hasn't pitched since that point. The good news is he's lined up to pitch on Saturday at Detroit's Comerica Park, which will surely be a feel good moment and send off for the likely future Hall of Famer. Verlander can also add a few more strikeouts to his career total of 3,554.

item.content:encoded:
The Mets have just nine games left in the season, and all of the attention is already shifting to the 2027 campaign. There are a lot of questions that the Mets have to answer this winter, and seeing the fans' over-the-top reaction to Pete Alonso's return this week shows how much work the front office needs to do to win back the trust of its fan base.
The free agent market is a bit thin this year, but it does have a few players who could help the Mets bolster their roster, particularly in the pitching department. That tally doesn't include Bo Bichette, whose opt-out decision will also play a significant role in how much money President of Baseball Operations David Stearns has to work with in free agency.
That said, let's dive into five potential free agents that the Mets should pursue this winter.
1. LHP Tarik Skubal
We took a deeper dive into the Tarik Skubal fit for the Mets last week, but it is fair to wonder if the fans' vitriolic display at Citi Field this week may inspire Steve Cohen to go for the top pitcher on the board as a make-good to them.
There are certainly injury risks with Skubal, but there isn't a better pitcher on the board, and his arrival would push the rest of the current rotation into more appropriate roles, starting with Nolan McLean as one of the best No. 2's in baseball.
2. LHP Robbie Ray
Skubal alone would bolster the Mets' rotation but Stearns should also look to add a veteran for the middle of the rotation who can give them quality innings. Enter Robbie Ray, a former Cy Young winner who is 13-8 with a 3.60 ERA in 30 appearances (including 29 starts) between the Giants and Padres.
The Mets would get a veteran lefty who has thrown at least 162.2 innings in four of the past six seasons, with the only exceptions being the 2022 and 2023 campaigns when he missed significant time rehabbing from Tommy John surgery. Putting Ray as the Mets' third starter would allow Stearns to bump Christian Scott down to the No. 4 spot and have healthy competition for the fifth between Sean Manaea, Jonah Tong, Zac Thornton and a slew of other depth options.
3. 1B/3B Alec Bohm
First base is one of the bigger questions on the Mets' roster, and they can't go into next season hoping that the combination of Jared Young, Mark Vientos, Brett Baty and Jorge Polanco can solve it. One good fit here could be Alec Bohm, who is hitting .251 with 15 home runs, 84 RBIs and a .707 OPS in 534 at-bats for the Phillies.
If the Mets feel like Young can be part of a first base platoon, then Bohm would make sense as a partner since he is very strong against lefties, batting .293 with seven homers, 36 RBIs and an .828 OPS against them in 179 at-bats. Veteran Paul Goldschmidt could also fill a platoon role with Young, but the Mets would be better served going with someone in his prime as opposed to a Goldschmidt-type towards the end of his career.
Bohm's ability to play both infield corners could also be helpful in the event Bichette opts out.
4. OF Ramon Laureano
The Mets' decision to move on from Tyrone Taylor (via trade) and Luis Robert Jr. (via waivers) has left them with an all-left-handed-hitting outfield of Juan Soto, A.J. Ewing and Carson Benge. While all three are capable starters, it would make sense to add a veteran option who can hit right-handed since Nick Morabito appears to need more minor league seasoning to be ready for that fourth outfielder role.
A good buy-low fit here could be Ramón Laureano, who has missed most of the season after undergoing surgery to repair a torn labrum in his right hip in May. Laureano can play both outfield corners and is just a year removed from a solid 2025 campaign where he hit .281 with 24 homers, 76 RBIs and an .855 OPS, so adding him on a one-year prove-it deal could give the Mets more flexibility to protect Juan Soto's health with DH days or sit one of Ewing or Benge against tough lefties.
5. RHP Evan Phillips
The Mets bullpen's strong performance post-deadline has lessened their need to go big-game hunting at the back end of the unit, but they still need to add a proven setup reliever to their mix. One name who could offer good value is Evan Phillips, who has pitched to a 3.68 ERA and 1.23 WHIP in 27 appearances for the Dodgers this season.
Phillips missed time with injuries this year but does have closing experience with Los Angeles, which could be valuable if Devin Williams struggles in his second year with the Mets. The injury issues Phillips had may drive his price down to a one- or two-year contract, which would be right up Stearns' wheelhouse and make him a good complement to the likes of Williams, Kodai Senga, Reed Garrett and Daniel Duarte in the relief mix.

item.content:encoded:
On the day of Carlos Beltran's number retirement ceremony at Citi Field, a special and joyous occasion for the club and all those involved, Mets owner Steve Cohen made sure to also address the elephant in the room – what's been bubbling up for many Mets fans this season, particularly this past week.
Speaking with the SNY booth in the fourth inning on Saturday, Cohen was asked about the recent shenanigans that happened at the ballpark during the team's last series with the Baltimore Orioles.
In what was Pete Alonso's first time back in Queens since he left the Mets in free agency over the offseason, fans came out in droves and gave the first baseman quite the reception. Not only did they give Alonso a standing ovation in his first at-bat, standard for a former beloved player coming back to his old ballpark, but fans were also actively cheering for Alonso's success every time he went to the plate.
Things got murky when Alonso, who was chasing his 300th career home run, hit the milestone by hitting a game-tying home run against Kodai Senga in the top of the ninth inning, which caused the stadium to erupt in cheers – odd for a home ballpark.
The Mets went on to lose that game in extra innings and during the postgame, players, including Sean Manaea, admitted to being surprised by the response of the home fans seemingly cheering against their team.
"You can't make it up, it was just so crazy," Cohen said on Saturday. "The fans, they're passionate and when they feel something they're gonna let you know and I'm okay with that. Pete hits his 300th home run and it was sort of poetic. It was sort of amazing that it all occurred at the same time."
Cohen seemed to understand where the fans were coming from, letting their frustration out for a player they believed deserved to be a lifetime Met.
Of course, that's not how things turned out, and in the midst of a disappointing season, it made it all the more painful.
"I'll say it again, it didn't surprise me," Cohen said about the fan's response to Alonso's return. "I can remember being at a previous Mets event the previous year and the fans were vocal on Alonso and listen, it's hard to say goodbye to a homegrown player. Obviously he's well liked and a great Met and those decisions got made and unfortunately we gotta look forward and look forward to '27 and what we're gonna do.
"But it was weird because we got past the trade deadline and the team was playing well and you got a sense that fans were really getting excited and then Pete came in and we kinda reversed course for three days, but now I think we're back on track again."
It's true, prior to Alonso's homecoming, despite the lost season, fans seemed to be invested in the team because of the young talent that spurred hope for the future, as well as the team's improved performance on the field, albeit too late.
Still, Cohen believed that what the Mets had been building was enough to garner enthusiasm for what's to come, even if it came during a second consecutive season missing the playoffs.
"I think that's what the fans like," he said. "We're playing young, we're playing athletic. We've developed a lot of players in a very short period of time and so that's something you can really look forward to. So it's true, two things can be true: a lousy season, but still something to look forward to."
Something else Mets fans can look forward to is help arriving for president of baseball operations David Stearns – both in terms of the front office as well as a manager.
Cohen talked about the search for somebody to lead the team and what he wants to see out of his next manager, a conversation that fittingly happened during Beltran's number retirement ceremony.
"I see the manager's role as mostly about culture and bringing the locker room together," the owner said. 'I think the actual managerial decisions are, I would say, 20-30 percent of what they do and the rest of it is trying to galvanize your ball club and trying to get them in the right frame of mind and I'm looking for someone that can bring out the best in their ball players."
As for the front office, Cohen mentioned that he's "identified some things that we can do better" and talked about bringing in extra voices to the mix to help out.
"We're going to try to add certain voices into the front office that I think will be helpful and I know David supports that, and I'm looking forward to, when we make those decisions, to announce them," he said.
Cohen continued: "It doesn't have to be a GM, it could be other ways to support David and the front office and I think the whole point is to get more opinions in the front office and people who are either pretty good at evaluating talent or people who have been in those positions before in the front office – in high positions – and help David out and help the team out as far as getting a different point of view."
Cohen was also asked how he deals with, as he described it, such passionate fans that are always eager to give their two cents in how to run the team.
"Everyone's got an opinion, I'll tell you that," he said. "…And frankly, there's some good ideas out there, so my ears are open."

item.content:encoded:
Since he hit Seth Lugo’s fastball, Yordan Alvarez knew that ball was out of the park. The hit came off at 107.2 mph and landed 385 feet into right field, right in the second-level seats at Daikin Park to give Houston a 4-1 lead over the Kansas City Royals earlier this week.
Thus continued Alvarez's pursuit of the Triple Crown—the last one was won by Miguel Cabrera in 2012 with the Detroit Tigers in the American League—, hitting his 40th home run of the season to join a select club in the history of the Astros and players born in Cuba.
He became just the fifth player in Astros history to reach that mark:
• Jeff Bagwell — 47 (2000), 43 (1997), 42 (1999)
• Lance Berkman — 45 (2006), 42 (2002)
• Richard Hidalgo — 44 (2000)
• Alex Bregman — 41 (2019)
• Yordan Alvarez — 40 (2026)
The Hall of Fame member, Jeff Bagwell, was the first Houston hitter to hit 40 or more home runs in a season, when he achieved the feat with 43 home runs in 1997, at 29 years old. In his entire career, he finished recording three similar seasons (1997, 1999 and 2000).
The 47 home runs he hit in the 2000 season remained marked as the most in club history. Richard Hidalgo (44 HR in 2000) and Alex Bregman (41 in 2019) have been the youngest hitters to enter the club, both at 25 years old. But this season, he has made the difference in an unprecedented season for a 40-home-run hitter who has worn the Astros uniform, as he leads the league with an offensive line of .311/.429/.598, 1.027 OPS, 189 OPS+, 319 total bases, 103 walks and 32 intentional walks.
After going through a slump in his home run production, with only five in the last 40 games, Alvarez has heated up again with a pair of home runs in his last 10 at-bats, both in the series that Houston won 2-1 against the Royals. Now he is one home run away from tying Tampa Bay Rays third baseman Junior Caminero, who leads the American League with 41, and three RBIs away from reaching Pete Alonso (102).
Houston has eight games remaining to finish the regular season, two more against the Atlanta Braves at home, a two-game road trip against the Seattle Mariners and four against the Athletics.
Another Chapter of Glory Among Cuban Hitters
Alvarez also joined the list of only four Cuban-born hitters who have hit at least 40 home runs in the Majors. The legendary Cooperstown Hall of Fame member, Tony Pérez, was the first Cuban-born hitter to hit at least 40 home runs in a season, when he reached the milestone in the 1970 season with the Cincinnati Reds’ “Big Red Machine.”
Eighteen years later, José Canseco appears on the historical list, at just 23 years old, in his historic 40-40 season (42 home runs and 40 stolen bases), wearing the Oakland Athletics uniform in 1988.
Canseco entered the club four times, repeating the feat with 41 home runs in 1991 and 46 in 1998. Another who reached the milestone was Rafael Palmeiro, who leads the group of Cuban hitters with four 40-home-run seasons (1998-1999 and 2000 and 2002). Seventeen years later, Jorge Soler hit 48 home runs with the Royals and took ownership of the record for Cubans in a single season, leaving behind Palmeiro’s 47-home-run seasons in 1999 and 2001.
For the first time in the club, Alvarez can go much farther if he manages to regain his home run pace in these last nine games. Before reaching the August and September stretch, his worst month in production had been June when he hit six home runs in 26 games. However, as we saw before, he has been able to take only five balls out of the park since August 1 until now, and that has made the race against Caminero become much more attractive.
Alvarez still has the possibility of reaching a Triple Crown by leading all three offensive categories in all of MLB, a feat that no hitter has accomplished since Mickey Mantle with the New York Yankees in 1956 (.353 BA, 52 HR, 130 RBI).

Join the dugout. Sign up here for Orioles updates in your inbox.
In the chaos that follows a momentous occasion such as this, major leaguers turn rowdy and the beer flows, or sprays, all over the walls. On this night, there was plenty of reason to be rowdy. Pete Alonso, the veteran force for the Orioles, joined an exclusive club by hitting his 300th home run.
Naturally, Alonso was thrown into a laundry cart and guided into the showers in the visiting clubhouse at Citi Field in New York. Beers cracked open, clothes became soaked and players hooted and hollered.
But right next to Alonso on Tuesday night, in a separate laundry cart at the eye of the storm, was a rookie reliever sharing in one of Baltimore’s largest celebrations this year. It was Alex Hoppe, the right-hander who arrived in a trade last month, celebrating his first career win.
“Baseball is a beautiful game sometimes,” left-hander Trevor Rogers said.
Long into the future, everyone in that shower-beer-party will remember whom they were celebrating. Alonso’s historic homer, yes. But also a rookie reliever’s first win. They’re at very different points in their careers — one reaching baseball immortality, the other just starting — but all milestones are worth celebrating.
Read More
“It’s such a baseball moment, and that’s why I love this game,” manager Craig Albernaz said. “You can have someone hit their 300th home run and also a reliever getting his first win as a rookie, and they’re both getting beer showers. … That’s what makes baseball great. You have those team moments, and you also recognize the ‘small’ individual accomplishments. Pete’s is big and Hoppe’s is not small, because every accomplishment in this league is big.”
That’s how Hoppe found himself right alongside Alonso with beer spraying all over.
And Alonso’s teammates weren’t surprised to see this slugger share the spotlight. Before they mobbed him, Alonso gave a speech.
“As easy as it can be to get wrapped up in a milestone like that, he talked to us postgame and said it was nothing about him. It was how good we did to come back after being down late,” Rogers said. “That’s the kind of guy he is, the kind of teammate he is. He could’ve not said anything about that. It was his 300th homer. But he’s just a team guy.”
On the field before Friday’s game, Hoppe said all the right things, too. He said the win matters most, and he was probably accurate when he said that in a month no fan will remember it was Hoppe who earned his first win that night.
At the same time, Hoppe will remember it. His family will remember it. Just as for his debut, and for his first save, Hoppe received a baseball from his outing. He also received a memory few people could even imagine.
“I think he can kind of hold that close to him for the rest of his life,” Coby Mayo said. “[Alonso’s] 300th career homer beer shower, and he’s right there alongside with him. Good for Hoppe.”
Hoppe arrived as part of the deal that sent outfielder Taylor Ward to the Seattle Mariners, and he has fit into this quirky bullpen group by following along and not questioning the weird traditions.
The 27-year-old tends to be a quiet figure. He does his work diligently. He chats here and there, but he’s not a boisterous guy like Rece Hinds and Colton Cowser. That is what makes him a fascinating fit for what Hoppe described as an “uncomfortable and cold” but incredible experience alongside Alonso.
Hoppe isn’t surprised, he said, that the Orioles remembered to celebrate him the same way for his first win.
“I think they just wanted another excuse to give another beer shower,” he joked.
But it’s not just that, even if that’s a big part.
“It speaks to the character and the group of guys we have in here,” Hoppe said. “Big accomplishments, small accomplishments, winning is hard and getting these accomplishments are hard and stuff, so it shows the true character of these guys and how we root for each other.”

item.content:encoded:
Yordan Alvarez has been the American League's best hitter in 2026. But is that enough for him to be crowned AL MVP? The Astros' designated hitter has one week left to hold off young Rays superstar Junior Caminero, who has made a surge for the award in recent weeks.
There's no denying that the Astros' slugger has had a monster season, hitting .311 with 40 homers and 99 RBI in 149 games entering Friday. He currently leads the AL in on-base percentage (.429), slugging (.598) and OPS (1.027). And he has stayed healthy and played in all but four of Houston's games, allowing him to put together a remarkable season.
When it comes to winning MVP, the numbers are critically important, and the narrative of the season plays a part as well. But an often overlooked aspect of award voting, particularly for MVP, is historical precedent.
Alvarez is a primary designated hitter, and prior to Shohei Ohtani's historic 50/50 season in 2024, in which he did not pitch but won NL MVP, no primary DH had ever won the MVP Award. Ohtani in 2024 is still the only DH to do it, given that in his other MVP seasons, he also pitched.
Considering his singular status as a two-way player, Ohtani is the exception to this rule. Besides him, no full-time designated hitter has ever won MVP. In fact, since 2000, only six designated hitters have finished in the top five of MVP voting. That list includes Frank Thomas (second in 2000, fourth in 2006), David Ortiz (fifth in 2003, fourth in 2004, second in 2005, third in 2006, fourth in 2007), Travis Hafner (fifth in 2005), J.D. Martinez (fourth in 2018), Marcell Ozuna (fourth in 2024) and Kyle Schwarber (second in 2025). Alvarez finished third in 2022 while splitting time between DH and outfield.
Among designated hitters since 1995, here are five of the top seasons comparable to Alvarez's 2026 and where they finished in MVP balloting:
- Edgar Martinez, 1995: .356/.479/.628, 182 H, 29 HR, 113 RBI, 182 wRC+, 7.0 fWAR — third
- Frank Thomas, 2000: .328/.436/.625, 191 H, 43 HR, 143 RBI, 160 wRC+, 5.9 fWAR — second
- David Ortiz, 2005: .300/.397/.604, 180 H, 47 HR, 148 RBI, 157 wRC+, 5.3 fWAR — second
- David Ortiz, 2007: .332/.445/.621, 182 H, 35 HR, 117 RBI, 175 wRC+, 6.3 fWAR — fourth
- J.D. Martinez, 2018: .330/.402/.629, 188 H, 43 HR, 130 RBI, 170 wRC+, 5.8 fWAR — fourth
- Yordan Alvarez, 2026: 311/.429/.598, 166 H, 40 HR, 99 RBI, 177 wRC+, 6.2 fWAR — ?
When you look at what Alvarez has accomplished this season, his numbers with eight games to play are right in line with those of his elite DH contemporaries. But if designated hitters who put up similar seasons weren't able to win MVP, will the Astros' slugger be able to reverse that trend?
Short of playing a defensive position, Alvarez has done everything he can to hold off Caminero, but the Rays' third baseman has made a push over the past month. The 23-year-old, who has earned the title of best player on the AL's best team, is slashing .277/.363/.532 with 41 home runs and 96 RBI this season. Although he rates out poorly defensively, Caminero has appeared in 151 games and counting at the hot corner. Plus, he delivered his potential MVP moment with a walk-off homer to clinch a playoff berth for the Rays.
One of the things working against Alvarez is the fact that, after being on pace to do so for most of the season, he is now unlikely to win the AL Triple Crown. Entering Friday, he's tied with Tampa Bay's Chandler Simpson for the league lead in batting average, he's second to Caminero in home runs, and he's second in RBI behind Baltimore's Pete Alonso.
Recent history tells us that a historic season, like Ohtani's 50/50 season in 2024 or Aaron Judge's AL-record 61 home runs in 2022, can provide the narrative juice to pave the way to MVP, making the Triple Crown Alvarez's best path to the award this year. Only Miguel Cabrera in 2012 has accomplished that feat in the past 60 years. Without the Triple Crown, it'll likely be tougher for Alvarez to sway voters.
Another thing that's likely hurting Alvarez's case is how poorly the Astros have played in 2026. They might be one of the worst division winners in MLB history, or they could still miss the postseason completely. That said, there's precedent for this in recent MVP voting, as Bryce Harper won the 2021 NL MVP Award on an 82-80 Phillies team that missed the postseason.
Over the past six seasons, the AL MVP Award has been dominated by Ohtani and Judge, with very little argument in the years they've won. But this season, with Alvarez and Caminero, voters will be selecting a new winner, and they'll have to decide what's most important in determining most valuable.
For the Astros' slugger, we'll wait to see if a nearly historic season by a designated hitter can be enough.

item.content:encoded:
The Triple Crown in the baseball world is a bit of an old-school feat, but it is a feat that very rarely happens these days, nonetheless. No hitter has won a Triple Crown since Miguel Cabrera pulled it off in 2012. Cabrera's feat was the first since 1967. A Triple Crown is leading your respective league in batting average, home runs and RBI. As noted, it's a bit old school because batting average isn't the most preferred rate stat and people have also shifted attention away from RBI.
Still, it's really cool to track when someone is close, and Astros outfielder and AL MVP frontrunner Yordan Alvarez has a real shot as the 2026 season winds down.
Heading into the penultimate weekend of the 2026 MLB season, here are the leaderboards, with Alvarez sitting in the top two of each category.
AL batting average leaders
1. Yordan Alvarez, Astros: .311 (.311444)
2. Chandler Simpson, Rays: .311 (.310661)
3. Yandy Díaz, Rays: .295
AL home run runs
1. Junior Caminero, Rays, 41
2. Yordan Alvarez, Astros, 40
3. Ben Rice, Yankees, 38
4. Pete Alonso, Orioles, 37
AL RBI leaders
1. Pete Alonso, Orioles, 102
2. Yordan Alvarez, Astros, 99
3. Junior Caminero, Rays, 96
4. Jo Adell, Guardians, 92
5. Ben Rice, Yankees, 92
As illustrated, all are tight races. It's possible Alvarez ends up leading the AL in none of the three categories, but he's right on the precipice of having a lead in all three.
Coincidentally, the last six Triple Crown winners in MLB have all been on the AL side. No National League player has won the Triple Crown since Hall of Famer Joe "Ducky" Medwick in 1937. Since then, the AL has seen Ted Williams (1942 and 1947), Mickey Mantle (1956), Frank Robinson (1966), Carl Yastrzemski (1967) and Miguel Cabrera (2012) pull it off.
No Astros player has ever won the Triple Crown.
Yordan Alvarez Triple Crown prediction
Could Alvarez become the first? The Astros -- who are clinging to the lead in the AL West -- and Alvarez have nine games remaining: they host the Braves for a three-game set this weekend before closing the regular season with a six-game road trip in Seattle (two games) and Sacramento (four games)
The two games in Seattle bring a difficult ballpark, but with three home games and finishing with four in Sacramento's Sutter Health Park, the conditions seem ripe for a strong finish. I'll predict that he gets the job done and wins the Triple Crown.
